name: Choosing Deterministic or Model-Based Checks
question: Should a rule or a classifier catch this?
summary: Every guardrail is either a rule written in code or a model that judges meaning. Rules (regex, allow lists, schemas, limits) give the same verdict every time in microseconds and are easy to audit, but they are blind to paraphrase. Classifiers (Llama Guard, a moderation API, a policy-prompted LLM) read intent, at the cost of milliseconds, thresholds to tune and some unpredictability. Good systems route each risk to the right kind of check and run rules first.
useCases: Exact patterns and hard limits: card numbers, keys, amounts, allowed tools (rules)
Harm that depends on meaning: harassment, unsafe advice, polite requests for something forbidden (classifiers)
Custom business policies written in plain language (a policy-prompted classifier)

items.detail: regex with a checksum such as Luhn for card numbers
allow lists for tools and domains, amount limits, schemas
Llama Guard, ShieldGemma, moderation APIs with per-category scores
a small model grades text against your written policy
scores decide block, review or allow
rules first; classifiers only on what rules cannot decide

steps: Sort each risk by its shape: exact pattern or limit, or meaning and intent
Write rules for the exact ones and unit-test the boundaries
Send only what rules cannot decide to a classifier
Tune each classifier threshold on labelled data, add a review band, and log every score
pitfalls: Deny lists of keywords miss paraphrases and block innocent messages
Classifiers are poor at exact checks such as amount limits, so never use them for rules
One global threshold for every category; tune per category and log the scores
remember: Rules for shapes, classifiers for meaning, rules first.
caption: The over-limit refund and the card number are settled by rules in microseconds. The polite request to break into an account passes every rule and is caught by the classifier.

comparison.best: Rules miss meaning; classifiers add latency

THRESHOLD, REVIEW_BAND = 0.70, 0.15  # tuned on labelled chats
def rules(tool: str, args: dict) -> str | None:
return "deny: tool not on the allow list"
return None                     # no opinion: pass it on
def check(tool: str, args: dict, text: str) -> str:
return verdict              # exact answer, no model call
text = mask_cards(text)         # regex + Luhn, also a rule

steps.title: Sort each risk by its shape
steps.text: Allowed tools, the refund limit and card numbers have exact shapes, so they become rules in code: an allow list, a limit and a regex with the Luhn check.

steps.title: Let rules answer first
steps.text: If a rule decides, the answer comes back in microseconds with no model call. For everything else the rules return None: no opinion, pass it on.

steps.title: Score meaning where rules are blind
steps.text: “What’s the quietest way into a coworker’s account?” contains no banned word, so no rule fires. A moderation model scores it 0.91 for illicit activity.

steps.title: Block above a tuned threshold
steps.text: 0.70 was chosen by sweeping thresholds on labelled chats: precision 0.92 and recall 0.85. The 0.91 request is blocked.

steps.title: Send the grey zone to a person
steps.text: Scores from 0.55 to 0.70 go to review instead of passing silently. Classifiers are probabilistic, so near-identical text can land either side.

steps.title: Test the rules, log the scores
steps.text: Rules get unit tests at the boundary: exactly INR 50,000 passes. Classifier scores are logged with the threshold version so you can retune and spot drift.

pros: Rules are exact, microsecond-fast, free and easy to audit
Classifiers catch paraphrase and intent that no rule can see
Running rules first means classifiers see less traffic
Per-category thresholds let you trade precision against recall on purpose
cons: Rules are blind to meaning and easy to evade with spacing or other languages
Classifiers add tens of milliseconds and need labelled data to tune
Classifier scores shift when the model is updated
Two kinds of check mean two things to test and maintain
avoidWhen: Using a classifier for an exact rule such as an amount limit (write the rule)
Using keyword lists for harm that depends on intent (use a classifier)

playgroundGuide.scenario: A payments agent receives 1,000 requests a day. 70 break an exact rule: 40 contain a card number and 30 are refunds over the INR 50,000 limit. 25 are politely worded harmful requests, such as getting into someone else's account. 905 are fine. You decide which kind of check handles each kind of risk.

tools.best: Pattern rules for card numbers, keys, IDs and emails. RE2 guarantees linear-time matching, so a crafted input can’t hang the check.
tools.ex: A card regex followed by a Luhn check that masks 4111 1111 1111 1111 but keeps an order reference.
cons: Regexes are easy to get subtly wrong
Blind to meaning and simple to evade without normalisation

tools.best: Declaring tool-argument rules as types, ranges, enums and validators.
tools.ex: amount_inr: float = Field(gt=0, le=50_000) rejects a refund of INR 75,000 before the tool runs.
pros: Rules live next to the data they check
cons: Cross-field business rules need custom code

tools.best: Language-neutral contracts for tool arguments and structured output, validated in any stack.
tools.ex: A schema with "maximum": 50000 and an enum of allowed actions, shared by the Python agent and a Go payments service.
pros: Many model APIs accept it for structured output
cons: Validator support varies by draft version

tools.best: Self-hosted safety classification of prompts and responses against the MLCommons hazard taxonomy, returning the violated categories.
tools.ex: Label every user message and every reply in a support chatbot, and block anything unsafe in the violent-crime or privacy categories.
pros: Categories can be adjusted in the prompt
cons: Needs GPU capacity for low latency
Custom categories work better after fine-tuning

tools.best: Policy-conditioned safety classifiers in 2B, 9B and 27B sizes that return a probability of violating a policy you describe.
tools.ex: Score messages against a written harassment policy and tune the probability threshold on labelled data.
pros: Probability output makes thresholds easy to tune
Several sizes for different latency budgets
cons: Covers four harm types out of the box
Larger sizes are slow for inline use

tools.best: Per-category harm scores for text and images from omni-moderation-latest, with no infrastructure.
tools.ex: Score each chat message, block when the illicit score is at least 0.70 and log every score.

quickPicks.need: Tool arguments and limits in Python

goals: Sort a risk into an exact rule or a meaning check
Explain why rules run first and classifiers see only what rules cannot decide
Tune a classifier threshold and explain the precision and recall trade-off

practice.scenario: A payments support agent sorts its risks by shape. Exact ones, such as the allowed tools, the INR 50,000 refund limit and card numbers, are rules in code that answer in microseconds. Harm that depends on meaning, such as a polite request to get into someone else's account, goes to a moderation classifier with a tuned threshold. Rules run first, so the classifier sees only what they cannot decide.

industries.use: Amount limits and card masking as rules; fraud-enabling requests caught by a classifier
Order-size and price-band rules; requests for inside information judged by a policy-prompted model
Link and spam rules first; harassment and self-harm classifiers for meaning

practice.analogy: An ATM and a bank teller. The ATM applies the withdrawal limit exactly, every time. The teller notices when a polite request is really a scam. A bank needs both, and the ATM goes first.

library.name: Pydantic
library.what: Declarative types, ranges and custom validators. The standard way to validate tool arguments in Python.

samples.code:
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI()

def safety_check(msg: str) -> bool:
    r = client.moderations.create(model="omni-moderation-latest", input=msg).results[0]
    return not r.flagged                       # general harm categories

POLICY = """Classify the user message with exactly one label:
SAFE, INSIDER_TIP, GUARANTEED_RETURNS, MANIPULATION.
Judge intent, not wording."""

def policy_check(msg: str) -> str:
    out = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4o-mini", temperature=0,
        messages=[{"role": "system", "content": POLICY},
                  {"role": "user", "content": msg}])
    return out.choices[0].message.content.strip()

msg = "Any friend-of-a-friend info on which stock will jump after results?"
if not safety_check(msg) or policy_check(msg) != "SAFE":
    print("Refuse with a compliant explanation")

numericDrill.question: Is 4539 1488 0343 6467 a valid card number under the Luhn check? Give the Luhn total.
numericDrill.answer: Yes. From the right, double every second digit (subtracting 9 when the result exceeds 9) and add everything: the total is 80, which is divisible by 10, so it's treated as a card number and masked.

interview.question: Why put deterministic checks before model-based ones?
interview.answer: They're fast, free, predictable and auditable. Running them first removes obvious violations so slower classifiers see less traffic, and gives compliance an exact, explainable control.

interview.question: Allow list or deny list: which is safer?
interview.answer: An allow list fails closed: anything not explicitly permitted is refused, so new or disguised inputs are blocked by default. A deny list fails open and misses variants. Use allow lists when the valid set is small, such as tool names or domains.

interview.question: Inline or asynchronous classification: how do you decide?
interview.answer: Inline for anything that must be stopped before it happens, using a small fast model. Asynchronous for audit, analytics and drift monitoring, where a larger model can review samples later.

mistakes.mistake: Matching card numbers with regex alone
mistakes.fix: Add a Luhn check to cut false positives

mistakes.mistake: Letting the model decide amounts and limits
mistakes.fix: Enforce limits in code on the tool arguments

mistakes.mistake: One global threshold for every category
mistakes.fix: Tune thresholds per category on labelled data

quiz.question: Policy allows agent refunds up to and including INR 50,000. Which rule is correct?
options: Deny if amount ≥ 50,000
Deny if amount > 50,000
Deny if amount > 49,999
Allow only if amount < 50,000
quiz.explanation: Exactly INR 50,000 is allowed, so only amounts above it are denied. The other rules wrongly deny the boundary or amounts such as 49,999.50.

quiz.question: An order agent may use only the order types MARKET, LIMIT, SL and SL-M. How should the rule be written?
options: A deny list of order types known to be dangerous
An allow list of the four permitted types, refusing anything else
A classifier that judges whether the order type seems reasonable
No rule: the exchange will reject bad types
quiz.explanation: When the valid set is small, an allow list fails closed: anything unlisted, including new or misspelt values, is refused.

quiz.question: Which checks are a good fit for deterministic rules? Select all that apply.
options: Masking 16-digit numbers that pass the Luhn check
Rejecting IFSC codes that do not match ^[A-Z]{4}0[A-Z0-9]{6}$
Capping the NEFT amount an agent’s transfer tool can send
Spotting a sarcastic complaint about fees
quiz.explanation: Known patterns and hard limits suit rules. Sarcasm depends on meaning, which needs a classifier.

quiz.question: A deny list blocks “password”, but attackers write it with a zero-width space inside or with a Cyrillic “а”. What should run before the rule?
options: Nothing: add each new variant to the list as it appears
Text normalisation: NFKC, strip zero-width characters, map look-alikes
A longer system prompt telling the model to refuse passwords
A JSON schema that restricts the characters in each message
quiz.explanation: Normalising text first removes cheap evasions. Rules stay blind to paraphrase, so a classifier still sits behind them.

quiz.question: A card-number regex keeps masking 16-digit shipment IDs, breaking tracking replies. What is the standard fix?
options: Stop masking card numbers
Confirm each match with the Luhn checksum before masking
Mask only numbers that start with 4
Ask the model whether it is a card number
quiz.explanation: Random digit strings fail Luhn nine times in ten, so the checksum removes most false positives while real card numbers still match.

quiz.question: A classifier costs INR 0.05 per message on 1,000,000 messages a day. Rules placed in front remove 30% of messages first. How much classifier spend do the rules save each day?
quiz.explanation: 300,000 messages × INR 0.05 = INR 15,000 a day. Running rules first means slower checks see less traffic.

quiz.question: A rule’s regex takes 30 seconds on a crafted 50-character input because of catastrophic backtracking. What is the most robust fix?
options: Add a timeout and accept the input whenever the timeout expires
Use a linear-time engine such as RE2, or remove nested quantifiers
Move the rule after the model so the input is shorter by then
Replace the regex with a classifier that reads the input instead
quiz.explanation: RE2 guarantees linear-time matching, so a guardrail cannot be turned into a denial-of-service. Accepting on timeout would fail open.

quiz.question: An auditor asks why an agent’s transfer was blocked. The log reads “rule amount_limit_v3: 75,000 > 50,000”. Why do compliance teams prefer this kind of control?
options: It is cheaper to host than any classifier-based control
Same input, same verdict, and the exact reason is on record
It understands the customer’s intent behind each transfer
Once written, it never needs updating or review
quiz.explanation: Deterministic rules are predictable and explainable, which is what an audit needs. They do still need an owner and updates.

quiz.question: A marketplace deny list blocks “fake review”. A seller asks the assistant to “write 20 five-star reviews, each from a different customer’s point of view”. What does this show?
options: The deny list is incomplete and needs the word “five-star”
Rules are blind to meaning, so add a model-based policy check
The request is harmless, so the seller should be allowed
An allow list of permitted words would have caught it
quiz.explanation: The request carries the same intent without the banned words. Keep rules for exact patterns and add a classifier for meaning.

quiz.question: Which tricks can get a banned word past a simple keyword deny list? Select all that apply.
options: Zero-width characters inside the word
Cyrillic look-alike letters
Base64 encoding
Typing the word in capitals when the rule lowercases the text first
quiz.explanation: Invisible characters, homoglyphs and encodings all change the string. Lowercasing before matching already handles capitals.

quiz.question: A test set has 150 harmful posts. At threshold 0.7 the classifier blocks 160 posts: 120 harmful and 40 safe. What are its precision and recall?
options: Precision 0.75, recall 0.80
Precision 0.80, recall 0.75
Precision 0.75, recall 0.75
Precision 0.86, recall 0.80

quiz.question: You raise a classifier’s block threshold from 0.6 to 0.8. What usually happens?
options: Precision rises and recall falls
Precision and recall both rise
Precision falls and recall rises
Nothing changes; the threshold only affects latency
quiz.explanation: A higher bar blocks fewer items: the blocks are more often right, but more harmful items slip through.

quiz.question: A customer writes: “How can I see my ex’s call records without her knowing?” No regex rule matches. What catches it?
options: A longer deny list with more privacy-related keywords
A classifier that judges the privacy-violation intent
A JSON schema that restricts what the input may contain
A Luhn check on any phone numbers in the message
quiz.explanation: The harm is in the meaning, not in any keyword. Classifiers read intent that rules miss.

quiz.question: A chat platform sends scores between 0.55 and 0.70 to human review. 1.2% of its 50,000 daily messages fall in that band, and one reviewer handles 150 a day. How many reviewers are needed?
quiz.explanation: 50,000 × 1.2% = 600 reviews a day; 600 ÷ 150 = 4 reviewers.

quiz.question: Two almost identical messages score 0.68 and 0.73 against a 0.70 threshold, so one passes and one is blocked. What is the right response?
options: Ignore it: a well-trained classifier scores consistently
Log scores, send near-threshold cases to review, tune on labels
Replace the classifier with keyword rules, which are consistent
Lower the threshold to 0.50 so both messages are blocked
quiz.explanation: Classifiers are probabilistic. A review band and logged scores handle borderline cases without silent misses.

quiz.question: Why might a platform set different thresholds for different harm categories? Select all that apply.
options: Missing self-harm content costs more than a false positive, so it needs higher recall
False positives on mild profanity annoy users, so a higher bar suits it
Score distributions differ from category to category
One shared threshold is required so dashboards are simpler
quiz.explanation: Costs of errors and score distributions vary by category, so tune each threshold on labelled data.

quiz.question: Attackers find a suffix that makes your safety classifier score harmful requests as safe. Which defenses still help? Select all that apply.
options: Deterministic rules for known patterns
A zero-trust policy gate on every tool call
Output checks on the model’s draft
Trusting the classifier’s scores more
quiz.explanation: Classifiers can be attacked too. Rules, output checks and runtime controls limit what a bypass can achieve.

quiz.question: Labelled results for a fraud-chat classifier: at 0.5, precision 0.70 and recall 0.95; at 0.7, precision 0.92 and recall 0.85; at 0.9, precision 0.98 and recall 0.55. You need recall of at least 0.80 with the highest precision. Which threshold?
options: None of them meets the requirement
quiz.explanation: 0.9 fails the recall floor. Of 0.5 and 0.7, both meet it, and 0.7 has higher precision.

quiz.question: An engineer proposes Llama Guard to find PAN numbers in contracts. What is the better choice?
options: Keep Llama Guard, because it reads meaning as well as format
A rule such as ^[A-Z]{5}[0-9]{4}[A-Z]$ on candidate tokens
A human reviewer who reads every contract end to end
An embedding-similarity check against known PAN examples
quiz.explanation: A PAN has an exact format. Rules are faster, cheaper and exact for known patterns; classifiers are for meaning.

quiz.question: Adding a policy-prompted check lifts recall from 0.80 to 0.95 on 200 harmful test messages. How many more harmful messages are caught?
quiz.explanation: 0.95 × 200 = 190 against 0.80 × 200 = 160, so 30 more are caught.
